Version, licence and every library the app is built from
Underlying audio system used for playback. Takes effect the next time the audio output is opened: at the next start, or when the output device changes.
Modern low-latency Android audio API. Available on Android 8.0+ (API 26+).
Legacy audio API. Deprecated in Android 13 but may help on older or problematic devices.
Puts the music in a room, whatever engine is playing it. The room rings on for a moment after the music stops, as a real one would.
How much of the room is heard against the music itself. The loudness stays the same all the way across; at 100% only the room is left.
A room about five metres long. Rings for about a second.
A room about ten metres long. Rings for about 1.3 seconds.
A room big enough for a band to play live in. Rings for about 1.5 seconds.
A medium-size concert hall. Rings for about 1.8 seconds.
A large concert hall with a long, even tail. Rings for about 4 seconds.
A stadium: a huge space whose sound takes seconds to die away. Rings for about 7 seconds.
The steel plate studios used before digital reverb: bright and dense, with no room behind it. Rings for about 1.3 seconds.
Small and tiled all round: close, bright and boomy. Rings for about 1.5 seconds.
Bare rock, whose treble rings on even longer than its bass. Rings for about 3 seconds.
Doubles the music with a copy of itself whose pitch drifts slowly up and down, for a thicker, wider sound. A mono tune comes out in stereo.
How fast the copy drifts. Slow is a gentle shimmer; towards 5 Hz it becomes a vibrato.
How differently the two sides drift. At 0% the copy sits in the middle; at 100% the sides drift against each other, as wide as it goes.
How much of the copy is heard. Around 50% is the classic chorus; at 100% only the drifting copy is left.

Opens the sound out beyond the speakers or headphones, as ModPlug Player\'s surround did: a delayed copy of the middle of the mix, added to one side and taken from the other. On a single speaker the music plays unchanged.
How strong the effect is. At 0% the music is untouched.
Ten bands an octave apart, each turned up or down by as much as 12 dB. Everything is turned down by as much as the most any frequency is boosted, so a boost never clips.
Up boosts the band, down cuts it. The middle leaves it as it is.
Lets Oboe choose the best available API. Recommended for most devices.
Restore the last queue and continue playback when the app opens.

Plays every track at the same loudness, whatever format or library it is. Each track is analysed in the background before it is played and keeps one fixed level from its first note. Volume settings and per-file boosts are ignored while this is on.
Ignored while Sound Check is on.
Audio buffer size. Smaller = lower latency but risk of glitches. Applies on next track.
Noise shaping applied when rendering 16-bit output.
Save current log file to Downloads
Every file type the app plays, by the library that plays it
OpenMPT Paula resampler with A1200 filter for Amiga modules.
OpenMPT Paula resampler with A500 filter for Amiga modules.
No interpolation: the sample as it is, steps and all. The least work of the five.
A windowed sinc over the neighbouring samples: the smoothest, and the most work.
Sample resampling mode. Amiga modes emulate the Paula chip.
Write logs to a file for export
Output bit depth. Applies on next track.
Audio output rate (Hz). Higher = better quality, more CPU. Applies on next track.
Smooths volume/panning transitions between notes. -1 = recommended default, 0 = off (may click), higher = softer ramps.
The overall look the app is drawn in.
Dark backgrounds and light text, in any UI style.
How much of what is behind Liquid Glass shows through it.
Glass bends the light at its edges, like real glass. Off, it is a plain blur.
Needs Android 13 or later. Here the glass is a plain blur.
How far the loudness analysis of the library has got.
Choose a folder to open it here.
Stereo width (%). 0 = mono, 100 = normal, 200 = extra wide.
Samsung\'s One UI 8.5 - rounded cards, a frosted floating tab bar and pop-ups at the bottom, within reach, in your device\'s colors.
Apple\'s iOS 26 - Liquid Glass bars that bend what is behind them, large titles, inset grouped lists, in your device\'s colors.
libopenmpt • Hively • AdPlug • NES • Game Boy • SNES
Scales this console before it reaches the output. 100 leaves it as the chip made it.
Where each voice sits. An NES mixes everything to one output and has no panning of its own, so the middle is exactly what the chip produced and these are the only thing that will ever move it.
The voices an NSF\'s expansion chip adds after the APU\'s - a VRC6 brings three, a Namco 163 eight. Which is which is the file\'s own business, and the playing file names them.
A Game Boy pans its four voices in hardware, so there is a real stereo image here to widen or collapse. 0 is mono, 100 as the tune wrote it, 200 twice as wide.
How far apart the two sides are. At 100% they are as the console plays them, at 0% the sound is mono, and above 100% wider still.
Softens the grit the games\' low-rate mixing leaves at the top, as the earlier GSF players could. Off, the sound is exactly what the console puts out.
Where each channel sits. At the middle a channel is where its game puts it - some games send a channel to one side themselves - and these move it from there, as far as all the way to a side.
How a voice\'s recording is read between the samples it has. A voice takes a change when it next starts a note; the square waves and the noise the console makes itself are not touched by it.
Each sample held until the next, which is all the console does: its own bright, gritty sound, edges and all.
The same held samples, without the aliasing that playing them at a higher rate than the console\'s adds.
A straight line from each sample to the next. Takes the hardest edges off.
The same lines, without the aliasing they leave.
A curve through four samples. Smooth, and softer than the console, less so than linear.
A windowed sinc over thirty-two samples. The cleanest: the recording\'s whole band and nothing above it. The most work.
Where each voice sits. At the middle a voice is where its game puts it - the console pans every one of them itself - and these move it from there, as far as all the way to a side.

Each game mixes its music on the console\'s signal processor, with code of its own. On, the emulator does that code over with its own version of it: several times faster, and very nearly the same, and for most games each voice of the music is a channel of its own to watch and to mute. Off, the processor runs the game\'s code as it is: exact, for several times the work, and the channels are the left and the right. Takes at once.
The console\'s own reverb, as the game set it.
MP3, FLAC, AAC, ALAC, Ogg Vorbis, Opus, Musepack, WavPack, WAV
How far apart the two sides are. At 100% they are as the record was mixed, at 0% the sound is mono, and above 100% wider still.
DSP, ADX, HPS, AST, AFC, DTK and more

The delay line the DSP runs in the console memory. Turning it off is done inside the chip, since by the time there is a stereo pair it is already mixed in. The music keeps its own volume either way, so fades still fade.
How a voice is read between the samples it actually has.
The four-tap table the hardware uses. The only accurate choice: the softness it puts on everything is a real part of how the machine sounds.
Nearest sample, no smoothing. The raw BRR data, edges and all.
A windowed sinc over the same four samples. Brighter than the hardware, which rolls the top off.
Scales the mix. 100 leaves it as the chip produced it.
The chip AdLib tunes are heard through. The channel view is measured on Nuked OPL3 whichever is chosen; on another one a muted channel is turned down at the chip rather than removed.
Cycle-accurate emulation of the YMF262. The most faithful, and the heaviest.
The OPL3 emulator from DOSBox. Lighter, and how DOS games sound in it.
Two emulated YM3812s. OPL2 only: a tune written for the OPL3 loses what only the OPL3 could do.
AdLibEmu, the emulator older versions of AdPlug used. OPL2 only.
Stereo width (%), on the same scale as libopenmpt. 0 = mono, 100 = half the Amiga\'s hard panning, 200 = the full Amiga spread.
Boost applied to the mix gain the tune loaded with. These formats are quiet.
No API key used to search.
Reset all settings to default values.

Shows elapsed time in milliseconds or bytes of audio instead of minutes and seconds, for placing loop points exactly.
This file does not say how long it is, so the length above is a guess. A length set here is kept for this file.
Playback that reaches B goes straight back to A. Set each from where playback is, then nudge it. A saved loop plays like a subsong: it can be starred and added to playlists.
This console has no settings of its own.
A file is offered to these libraries in this order, and the first to recognise its contents plays it. An extension listed under two of them goes to whichever of the two recognises the file first.
Tracker modules from the Amiga, DOS and Windows: ProTracker, FastTracker, Scream Tracker, Impulse Tracker, OpenMPT and dozens more.
AHX and HivelyTracker songs: the Amiga\'s synthesised chiptunes.
Modules from Furnace and DefleMask, the chiptune trackers for dozens of consoles and computers.
Commodore 64 music, played on an emulation of the SID chip.
Game Boy Advance music, the games\' own sound code run on mGBA\'s emulation of the console.
Nintendo DS music, the games\' own sound code run on vio2sf: the DeSmuME emulator cut down to the console\'s sound.
Nintendo 64 music, the games\' own sound code run on lazyusf2: the Mupen64Plus emulator cut down to the console\'s sound.
PlayStation music, the games\' own sound code run on aopsf: Audio Overload\'s emulation of the console, with the sound unit of Highly Experimental.

Recorded music: MP3, FLAC, every kind of AAC, ALAC, Ogg Vorbis, Opus, Musepack, WavPack, WAV and AIFF, read and decoded by FFmpeg\'s demuxers and decoders - an audio-only build of it. Played from the file as it lies rather than read whole, with the words where the file carries them.

GameCube music streams in every container the games keep them in - Nintendo\'s DSP ADPCM with its standard header or a game\'s own (STM, IDSP, Cstr, RS03 and more), HAL\'s HPS, CRI\'s ADX, Nintendo\'s AST and AFC, the DVD\'s DTK streams, Hudson\'s PDT - with the left and the right of a split pair played together. Formats and codecs ported from vgmstream.
Ron Klaren\'s music from Amiga games, played with Ivo Zoer\'s replay routine.
Sound chip logs: Sega, NEC, MSX, the Yamaha FM family and dozens of arcade chips (VGM), the PC-98 (S98), AdLib captures from DOSBox (DRO) and the Mega Drive (GYM).
Console music: the NES and Famicom (NSF, NSFE), the Super Nintendo (SPC) and the Game Boy (GBS).
AdLib and Sound Blaster FM music from DOS games and trackers.
